intuition.summary: A regular sequence is a list of 'independent' equations: each new element avoids every zero-divisor left by the earlier ones, so each step cuts the module down as much as possible (dimension drops by exactly one).

Depth is a dimension-like invariant measured 'from big to small' (how many successive cuts one can make), always bounded by dimension; CM means this algebraic count agrees with the geometric dimension.
intuition.source: C. Ji, Cohen-Macaulay rings and schemes, §1.2

intuition.summary: CM rings share 'some of the algebro-geometric properties of a smooth variety', notably local equidimensionality; geometrically: no embedded points and no components of different dimension through a point, no 'fat' lower-dimensional parts.
intuition.source: Wikipedia 'Cohen-Macaulay ring' (intro and Geometric interpretation); Ji §2.2

intuition.summary: Depth 0 at the maximal ideal means m is associated: some nonzero element is killed by m, i.e. the closed point is an embedded component; a line with an embedded point has depth 0 but dimension 1.

Depth >= 2 is a Hartogs phenomenon: H^0_m and H^1_m vanish so M equals its sections on the punctured spectrum; S_2 modules are determined by their behaviour in codimension 1 (sections extend across codimension-2 closed sets).
intuition.source: K. Schwede, Math 7830 notes 2/24/2017, Lemma 0.2, Thm 0.3, Remark 0.4

intuition.summary: 'Hidden flatness': under mild hypotheses a local ring is CM iff it is a finite free module over a regular (e.g. polynomial / Noether normalisation) subring; geometrically all fibres of a finite map to affine space have the same degree.

motivation.summary: Origin is the unmixedness theorem: Macaulay (1916) for polynomial rings, Cohen (1946) for power series rings: an ideal generated by as many elements as its height has no embedded components. CM rings are exactly those where unmixedness holds.
motivation.source: Encyclopedia of Mathematics 'Cohen-Macaulay ring'; Wikipedia 'Cohen-Macaulay ring' (History)

motivation.summary: Terminology was unsettled in the 1950s-60s ('semi-regular', 'Macaulay', 'Macaulay-Cohen'); Northcott-Rees linked irreducibility of s.o.p. ideals to the CM property; homological methods of Auslander-Buchsbaum and Serre around 1956-57 gave the modern depth treatment.
motivation.source: C. Huneke, Hyman Bass and ubiquity: Gorenstein rings, §'Commutative algebra circa 1960'

motivation.summary: Depth was introduced through homological algebra; Bruns-Herzog present it as the most basic invariant after dimension, defined via regular sequences but detected by Ext vanishing, linked to projective dimension, with grade as the global version via Koszul complexes.
motivation.source: Bruns-Herzog, Ch. 1 summary (Cambridge Core chapter page)

motivation.summary: Auslander-Buchsbaum (1957, Trans. AMS 85, Thm 3.7) relating pd and depth; leads to Serre's homological characterisation of regular local rings (finite global dimension) and localisation of regular rings.

Geometric payoff: Serre duality holds in its clean form exactly for CM schemes (dualizing complex is a single sheaf); intersection multiplicity equals length when local rings are CM; Stanley used CM Stanley-Reisner rings (Reisner) to prove the Upper Bound Theorem for spheres.
motivation.source: Ji §3.1-3.2; Wikipedia 'Cohen-Macaulay ring' (Intersection theory, Coherent duality)

motivation.summary: Modern drivers: existence of big / maximal CM modules and complexes is tied to Hochster's homological conjectures, settled in mixed characteristic via perfectoid methods (André, Bhatt), with applications to birational geometry.

definitions.summary: M-regular sequence: x_1 non-zero-divisor on M, each x_i non-zero-divisor on M/(x_1..x_{i-1})M, and M/(x)M != 0. Hochster calls the version without the last condition 'possibly improper'; Wikipedia notes only some authors require the nonvanishing.
definitions.source: Bruns-Herzog Def 1.1.1 (chapter page); Hochster 615 supplement; Wikipedia 'Regular sequence'

definitions.summary: Depth (grade) of M on I: common length of maximal M-regular sequences in I (Rees); equals min{i : Ext^i(R/I,M) != 0}. Proof: induction on a maximal sequence using the long exact Ext sequence and that Ext^i(R/I,M) is killed by I; base case uses that a module with I in a zero-divisor set has I inside an associated prime.
definitions.source: Weibel Thm 4.4.8; Ogus notes Thm 0.2(2); Guan-Hu §3 Thm 3.1

definitions.summary: Depth via local cohomology: depth M = least n with H^n_m(M) != 0 (Weibel 4.6.3), and H^q_m(M) vanishes outside depth <= q <= dim; local cohomology is the colimit of Koszul cohomology on powers x^l, linking the Koszul and Ext definitions.

Depth via Koszul complex: for x generating I (n elements), depth_I M = n - max{q : H_q(x;M) != 0}; acyclicity of the Koszul complex on a regular sequence (Weibel 4.5.4) is the key step. The exact formula is from memory; Ji Thm 1.12 and Weibel §4.5 were seen only in outline.
definitions.source: Weibel §4.5; Ji Thm 1.12 (Koszul cohomology detects maximal regular sequence length)

definitions.summary: Lean formalisation takes the Ext definition (least i with Ext^i(N,M) != 0, else infinity) as primary and proves equality with sup of regular-sequence lengths as a theorem.

CM local ring/module: depth = dim (dim of support for modules); equivalently some (every) system of parameters is a regular sequence; equivalently Ext^i(k,R) or H^i_m(R) vanish for i < dim R; equivalently there is a regular sequence a_1..a_k with R/(a) Artinian.
definitions.source: Encyclopedia of Mathematics; Hochster 615 supplement §5; Stacks Def 10.103.1

definitions.summary: Global: a Noetherian ring/module is CM if all localisations at maximal ideals (equivalently all primes) are CM; Stacks proves localisation preserves CM (Lemma 10.103.11) so the two agree.

Maximal Cohen-Macaulay: depth M = dim R (Stacks Def 10.103.8), equivalently CM with dim M = dim R; the IMSW survey extends to complexes and separates 'big CM' (no finiteness) from MCM (finitely generated homology).
Hilbert-Samuel characterisation: R CM iff length(R/Q) = e(Q) for every (equivalently some) parameter ideal Q.
Serre's conditions: (S_k) depth A_p >= min(k, dim A_p) for all p, (R_k) A_p regular for ht p <= k; reduced iff R0+S1, normal iff R1+S2 (Krull for domains, Serre in general), CM iff S_k for all k.
definitions.source: Wikipedia 'Serre's criterion for normality'; Schwede notes Def 0.1

definitions.summary: Gorenstein glimpse: local ring of finite injective dimension; equivalently Ext^i(k,R)=0 for i != d and one-dimensional for i=d; Artinian reduction has simple socle; canonical module is R. Gorenstein implies CM (Weibel Cor 4.4.10); chain regular => c.i. => Gorenstein => CM, none reversible.

viewpoints.summary: Element-wise/algebraic: regular sequences and systems of parameters (Matsumura §16-17, Hochster notes).
Homological: depth as first non-vanishing Ext^i(k,M); Auslander-Buchsbaum pd M + depth M = depth R; regular iff finite global dimension (Weibel 4.4.15-16).

Cohomological/geometric: depth via H^i_m, CM = local cohomology concentrated in degree dim; for projective X with ample L, the section ring is CM iff intermediate cohomology H^i(X,L^j) vanishes (arithmetically CM).
viewpoints.source: Weibel §4.6; Wikipedia 'Cohen-Macaulay ring' (Section rings); EoM (arithmetically CM)

viewpoints.summary: Finite flat / Noether normalisation: CM iff free over a polynomial (regular) subring; graded case via homogeneous s.o.p.
Duality: CM iff dualizing complex is a single sheaf (shifted canonical module); Gorenstein iff that sheaf is a line bundle.
Combinatorial: Stanley-Reisner ring K[Delta] has dim = dim Delta + 1; CM iff Reisner's link-homology criterion; h-vector of CM complex is an O-sequence.
Categorical/representation-theoretic: MCM modules over Gorenstein rings form a Frobenius category whose stable category is the singularity category; over hypersurfaces MCM = matrix factorizations.

conventions.summary: Depth vs grade: Weibel writes G(A) ('grade') for the m-depth; Stacks/most papers write depth; Bruns-Herzog use grade(I,M) for the I-depth and depth M for the m-depth (BH split partly unverified).

Regular sequence nonvanishing condition M/(x)M != 0: required by Bruns-Herzog, Ogus, Hochster ('regular' vs 'possibly improper'); optional per Wikipedia; Guan-Hu/Mathlib distinguish 'weakly regular' (no condition) from 'regular'.
conventions.source: Hochster 615 supplement; Ogus notes; Wikipedia 'Regular sequence'; Guan-Hu §2.4

conventions.summary: Depth of zero module / IM = M: Wikipedia and Ogus set depth = infinity (Ogus: infinity when E/IE = 0); Guan-Hu: depth infinity when all Ext vanish, and zero module is CM by convention; Wikipedia's CM article also declares 0 CM; Stacks Def 10.103.1 states no zero-module convention.
conventions.source: Wikipedia 'Regular sequence'; Ogus; Guan-Hu §3-4; Wikipedia CM

conventions.summary: Serre (S_n): Schwede uses depth M_q >= min(n, dim R_q) and footnotes that some authors use dim M_q; Ficarra uses min(r, dim M_P) over Supp M; other sources phrase with ht p (equivalent for rings). Matters for modules without full support.
conventions.source: Schwede notes Def 0.1 footnote; Ficarra arXiv:2602.17240 §3

conventions.summary: 'Maximal Cohen-Macaulay': Stacks/Guan-Hu: finite with depth = dim R; IMSW: big CM complex with finitely generated homology; 'big CM' for non-finitely-generated modules (some require mM != M).
CM for non-local rings: localisation at all maximal ideals (Wikipedia, Hochster) vs all primes (Guan-Hu Def 4.11, Stacks 10.103.12); equivalent because CM localises.
Module dimension: dim Supp M = dim R/Ann M; dimension of zero module -infinity (Ficarra) vs undefined/left out.

examples.summary: CM: regular local rings (Z, k[x_1..x_n], power series), Artinian rings, reduced 1-dimensional rings, normal 2-dimensional rings, complete intersections, Gorenstein rings, invariant rings of linearly reductive groups (Hochster-Roberts), determinantal rings of expected codimension, normal toric/affine semigroup rings (Hochster), Grassmannians, Schubert varieties.
k[x]/(x^2): depth 0 = dim 0, CM but not reduced; k[t^2,t^3] (cusp) Gorenstein non-regular; k[t^3,t^4,t^5] CM not Gorenstein; k[x,y]/(x,y)^2 CM, socle of dimension 2 so not Gorenstein.
examples.source: Wikipedia CM and Gorenstein articles; Huneke (monomial curves symmetric semigroup)

examples.summary: Standard non-example: k[x,y]/(x^2,xy) (line with embedded point at origin): dim 1, depth 0 at origin. Used by Wikipedia (Depth, CM), Ji, Hochster.
Non-equidimensional: k[x,y,z]/(xy,xz) (= (x) cap (y,z): plane union line) reduced but not CM; Hochster's K[[x,y,z]]/((x,y) cap (z)) catenary but not equidimensional.

Two planes meeting in a point, k[w,x,y,z]/(wy,wz,xy,xz): reduced, equidimensional, still not CM (Hartshorne connectedness / depth 1). Affine cones over abelian varieties of dim >= 2 not CM; Segre products of CM rings need not be CM.
Regular sequence order matters globally: x, y(1-x), z(1-x) regular in k[x,y,z] but y(1-x), z(1-x), x not (Wikipedia); Hochster's version x-1, xy, xz; permutation is fine in local or graded settings.
Z_(p) has depth 1; k[x_1..x_n] localised at the origin has depth n; k[x,y,z]/(x^2,yz) is CM (Ji).
K[[x^2,x^3,y^2,y^3]] is CM but not normal; a Segre product (cubic cone x P^1) gives a normal domain that is not CM - so S2 (normal) does not imply CM in dim >= 3.

computation.summary: Find an explicit maximal regular sequence (check each element is a non-zero-divisor modulo the previous; in graded/local case order is irrelevant); in practice a homogeneous s.o.p. of a graded ring is regular iff the ring is CM.

Auslander-Buchsbaum: over a regular (polynomial) ring S, depth M = dim S - pd_S M, read off from the length of a minimal free resolution; Wikipedia calls it a practical way to compute depth; A CM iff pd_S A = codim A.
Ext / Koszul computation: depth = first i with Ext^i(k,M) != 0, or n minus top nonvanishing Koszul homology on generators of m; local cohomology via Cech/Koszul colimit.

Depth lemma and quotient by regular element: depth drops by exactly 1 modulo a regular element; short exact sequences give inequalities depth B >= min(depth A, depth C) etc.; used to propagate depth through exact sequences (Ohtani-type decompositions in combinatorial papers).
computation.source: Guan-Hu Lemma 3.5, Thm 3.6; Stacks Lemma 10.72.6-10.72.7 cited in proof of 10.111.1

computation.summary: Graded/Hilbert series test: for CM graded K-algebras, Hilbert series times (1-t)^d is the h-polynomial with nonnegative coefficients (O-sequence); Stanley-Reisner rings via Reisner's criterion on links.
Software: Macaulay2 Depth package provides depth, isCM, isRegularSequence, regularSequenceCheck, systemOfParameters.

confusions.summary: 'Regular sequences can be permuted' is false in general (non-local, non-graded): Wikipedia's and Hochster's examples; true for elements of m over a local ring or homogeneous positive degree elements in graded case.
Equidimensional + reduced does not imply CM (two planes meeting in a point); normal does not imply CM in dim >= 3 (Segre product example; affine cone over abelian surface).

depth <= dim M <= dim R, and more sharply depth M <= dim R/p for every associated prime p; so CM modules have no embedded primes and all associated primes are minimal (Ogus 0.2(3), Stacks 10.103.7, Guan-Hu Cor 3.13).
confusions.source: Ogus notes; Stacks Lemma 10.103.7; Guan-Hu Cor 3.13

confusions.summary: CM is not 'smooth': k[x]/(x^2) and the cusp are CM; smooth => regular => CM but the converses fail.

Global CM rings need not be equidimensional across components (e.g. k[x] x k[y,z]) - CM is a local condition; equidimensionality/catenarity hold locally. (unverified: this specific example is from memory)
MCM over regular local rings are free (Auslander-Buchsbaum), so the interesting theory of MCM modules lives over singular rings (hypersurfaces, matrix factorizations).
Depth of a module depends on the ideal: m-depth vs I-depth; papers fix m-depth for finite modules over local rings (Holanda-Miranda-Neto convention).
